caption:
At the peak of Japan's 1980s bubble, the grounds of the Imperial Palace alone were valued higher than all of California — and the city's most iconic mountain view isn't even inside city limits. 👀

Comment your guess for which fact surprised you most before you swipe ⬇️

1. Imperial Palace
At the peak of Japan's 1980s real estate bubble, the grounds of the Imperial Palace — just 1.32 square miles — were valued higher than all real estate in California combined.

2. Senso-ji
Senso-ji in Asakusa was nearly destroyed in WWII Allied firebombing raids that killed over 80,000 people in a single night — the deadliest bombing raid in history. The temple was rebuilt, and today receives 30 million visitors a year.

3. Shibuya Crossing
Up to 2,500 people cross Shibuya Crossing simultaneously from every direction, with zero collisions. No designated lanes, no enforced paths. It just works.

4. Shinjuku Station
Shinjuku Station serves over 3.5 million passengers daily. First-time visitors routinely get lost for hours and locals give directions by exit number, not street names — the station has around 200 exits.

5. Tokyo Tower
Tokyo Tower was deliberately modeled on Paris's icon. It was built in 1958 as a symbol of Japan's post-war rebirth, and it stands 13 meters taller than its inspiration.

6. Edo
For centuries Tokyo was called Edo — a small fishing village that grew into the world's largest city by the 1720s, a full century before London or New York came close. The name only changed to Tokyo in 1868.

7. Mount Fuji
On clear days you can see Mount Fuji from the city. It's been an active volcano for 100,000 years, last erupted in 1707, and is still classified as potentially active today.
